Hint: Consider the subsequences \(X_i,X_{i+m+1},X_{i+2(m+1)},\ldots\) for \(1\le i\le m+1\).

(b) Suppose that \(\{X_n\}\) are iid and each \(X_i\) has finite range \(x_1,\ldots,x_l\) and

\[
P[X_1=x_i]=p(x_i),
\qquad
i=1,\ldots,l.
\]

For \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\), a \(k\)-tuple of the \(x_i\)'s, let \(N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\) be the frequency of the \(k\)-tuple in the first \(n+k-1\) trials; that is, the number of \(m\) such that \(1\le m\le n\) and

\[
X_m=u_1,\ldots,X_{m+k-1}=u_k.
\]

Show that with probability \(1\), all asymptotic relative frequencies are what they should be—that is, with probability \(1\),

\[
n^{-1}N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)
\to
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)
\]

for every \(k\) and every \(k\)-tuple \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\).
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

#### (a)

Since \(\{X_n\}\) are uniformly bounded, there exists \(M<\infty\) such that

\[
\sup_n\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\le M.
\]

For each \(i=1,\ldots,m+1\), consider the subsequence

\[
Z_{i,r}
=
X_{i+(r-1)(m+1)},
\qquad
r\ge1.
\]

Any two variables in this subsequence are more than \(m\) positions apart. Therefore, for each fixed \(i\), the sequence \(\{Z_{i,r}\}_{r\ge1}\) is independent.

Also,

\[
E(Z_{i,r})=0,
\]

and

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{Z_{i,r}}r\right)
=
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z_{i,r})}{r^2}
\le
M\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac1{r^2}
<
\infty.
\]

By the Kolmogorov convergence criterion,

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{Z_{i,r}}r
\]

converges almost surely. Hence, by Kronecker's lemma,

\[
\frac1q\sum_{r=1}^qZ_{i,r}
\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

For each \(n\), let

\[
N_i(n)
=
\#\left\{
r\ge1:
i+(r-1)(m+1)\le n
\right\},
\]

and define

\[
S_i(n)
=
\sum_{r=1}^{N_i(n)}Z_{i,r}.
\]

Notice that

\[
\frac{N_i(n)}n\to\frac1{m+1}.
\]

Also, since \(N_i(n)\to\infty\),

\[
\frac{S_i(n)}{N_i(n)}
\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{S_i(n)}n
=
\frac{N_i(n)}n
\frac{S_i(n)}{N_i(n)}
\to
\frac1{m+1}\cdot0
=
0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

The \(m+1\) subsequences partition \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), so

\[
S_n
=
\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}S_i(n).
\]

Thus,

\[
\left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right|
\le
\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}
\left|\frac{S_i(n)}n\right|
\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Hence,

\[
\frac{S_n}{n}\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

#### (b)

Fix \(k\ge1\) and a \(k\)-tuple \((u_1,\ldots,u_k)\). Define

\[
Y_m
=
1_{\{X_m=u_1,\ldots,X_{m+k-1}=u_k\}},
\qquad
m\ge1.
\]

Then

\[
N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)
=
\sum_{m=1}^nY_m.
\]

By independence of the \(X_i\)'s,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E(Y_m)
&=
P(X_m=u_1,\ldots,X_{m+k-1}=u_k)\\
&=
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k).
\end{aligned}
\]

The variable \(Y_m\) depends only on

\[
X_m,\ldots,X_{m+k-1}.
\]

Therefore, \(Y_m\) and \(Y_j\) are independent whenever

\[
|j-m|\ge k.
\]

Thus, the sequence \(\{Y_m\}\) is \((k-1)\)-dependent. Since \(0\le Y_m\le1\), the centered sequence

\[
Y_m-E(Y_m)
\]

is uniformly bounded, has mean zero, and is \((k-1)\)-dependent.

By part (a),

\[
\frac1n
\sum_{m=1}^n
\left(Y_m-E(Y_m)\right)
\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(E(Y_m)=p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)\),

\[
\frac{N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)}n
-
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)
\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore, for every fixed \(k\) and every fixed \(k\)-tuple,

\[
\frac{N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)}n
\to
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

For each \(k\) and each \(k\)-tuple \(\mathbf u=(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\), let

\[
A_{k,\mathbf u}
=
\left\{
\frac{N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)}n
\to
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)
\right\}.
\]

We have

\[
P(A_{k,\mathbf u})=1.
\]

Since the range \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_l\}\) is finite, the collection

\[
\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}
\{x_1,\ldots,x_l\}^k
\]

of all finite tuples is countable. Hence,

\[
P\left(
\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}
\ \bigcap_{\mathbf u\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_l\}^k}
A_{k,\mathbf u}
\right)
=
1.
\]

Thus, with probability \(1\),

\[
\frac{N_n(u_1,\ldots,u_k)}n
\to
p(u_1)\cdots p(u_k)
\]

for every \(k\) and every \(k\)-tuple \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\).

### Ex 12

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n\}\) is defined iteratively in the following way: Let \(X_0\) have a uniform distribution on \([0,1]\) and for \(n\ge1\), \(X_{n+1}\) has a uniform distribution on \([0,X_n]\). Show that

\[
\frac1n\log X_n
\]

converges a.s. and find the almost sure limit.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Firstly, we can investigate the expectation of \(\log X_n\).

Since \(X_0\) is uniform on \([0,1]\),

\[
E(\log X_0)
=
\int_0^1\log x\,dx
=
-1.
\]

The calculations suggest that

\[
E(\log X_n)=-(n+1),
\]

and hence

\[
E\left(\frac{\log X_n}{n}\right)
=
-\frac{n+1}{n}
\to-1.
\]

Therefore, we guess that

\[
\frac{\log X_n}{n}\to-1
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

To prove this, define

\[
U_i=\frac{X_i}{X_{i-1}},
\qquad i\ge1.
\]

Since \(X_i\), conditional on \(X_{i-1}=x\), is uniform on \([0,x]\), for \(0\le u\le1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(U_i\le u\mid X_0,\ldots,X_{i-1})
&=
P\left(
X_i\le uX_{i-1}
\mid X_0,\ldots,X_{i-1}
\right)\\
&=
u.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus, the conditional distribution of \(U_i\) is uniform on \([0,1]\) and does not depend on the past. Therefore, \(\{U_i\}\) are iid uniform random variables on \([0,1]\).

Now,

\[
X_n
=
\frac{X_n}{X_{n-1}}
\frac{X_{n-1}}{X_{n-2}}
\cdots
\frac{X_1}{X_0}X_0
=
X_0\prod_{i=1}^nU_i.
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
\log X_n
=
\log X_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\log U_i.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{\log X_n}{n}
=
\frac{\log X_0}{n}
+
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log U_i.
\]

Since \(X_0>0\) almost surely,

\[
\frac{\log X_0}{n}\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Also,

\[
E|\log U_1|
=
\int_0^1|\log u|\,du
=
1
<
\infty,
\]

and

\[
E(\log U_1)
=
\int_0^1\log u\,du
=
-1.
\]

Hence, by the SLLN,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log U_i
\to
E(\log U_1)
=
-1
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\log X_n}{n}\to-1
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]


### Ex 16

::: problem
If \(\{X_n\}\) are iid with \(E|X_1|<\infty\) and \(EX_1\ne0\), show that

\[
\frac{\displaystyle\bigvee_{i=1}^n|X_i|}
{\displaystyle\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|}
\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,
\qquad
M_n=\max_{1\le i\le n}|X_i|,
\qquad
\mu=E(X_1)\ne0.
\]

We have

\[
\frac{M_n}{|S_n|}
=
\frac{M_n}{n}\frac{n}{|S_n|}.
\]

By the SLLN,

\[
\frac{S_n}{n}\longrightarrow\mu
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(\mu\ne0\),

\[
\frac{n}{|S_n|}
=
\frac1{|S_n/n|}
\longrightarrow
\frac1{|\mu|}
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore, we only need to discuss

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{n}.
\]

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), since \(E|X_1|<\infty\),

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon n)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
P(|X_1|>\varepsilon n)
<
\infty.
\]

By Borel--Cantelli,

\[
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon n\text{ i.o.})=0.
\]

That is, with probability one, there exists \(N\) such that for every \(i\ge N\),

\[
|X_i|\le i\varepsilon.
\]

Hence, for \(n\ge N\),

\[
|X_i|\le i\varepsilon\le n\varepsilon,
\qquad
N\le i\le n.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
M_n
&=
\max\left\{
\max_{1\le i<N}|X_i|,
\max_{N\le i\le n}|X_i|
\right\}\\
&\le
\max\left\{
\max_{1\le i<N}|X_i|,
n\varepsilon
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since

\[
\max_{1\le i<N}|X_i|
\]

is a finite random variable that does not depend on \(n\), we have

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{n}
\le\varepsilon
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Now take \(\varepsilon=1/r\), \(r\in\mathbb N\), and intersect the corresponding probability-one events. We obtain

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n}{n}
\le\frac1r
\]

for every \(r\ge1\), almost surely. Since \(M_n/n\ge0\),

\[
\frac{M_n}{n}\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\frac{M_n}{|S_n|}
=
\frac{M_n}{n}\frac{n}{|S_n|}
\longrightarrow
0\cdot\frac1{|\mu|}
=
0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

### Ex 35

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) is iid and

\[
E(X_1^+)<\infty,
\qquad
E(X_1^-)=\infty.
\]

Show

\[
\frac{S_n}{n}\to-\infty
\]

almost surely. (Try truncation of \(X_n^-\) and use the classical SLLN.)
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,
\qquad
\mu^+=E(X_1^+)<\infty.
\]

For \(K\in\mathbb N\), define

\[
Y_i^{(K)}
=
X_i^-1_{\{X_i^-\le K\}},
\qquad
\mu_K=E(Y_1^{(K)}).
\]

For each fixed \(K\), the random variables
\(\{Y_i^{(K)}\}\) are iid and bounded. Therefore, by the SLLN,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i^{(K)}
\to\mu_K
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Also, since \(E(X_1^+)<\infty\), the SLLN gives

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^+
\to\mu^+
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(K\in\mathbb N\), we may take a countable intersection of the corresponding probability-one events. Thus, with probability one, all the above convergences hold simultaneously for every \(K\in\mathbb N\).

Since

\[
Y_i^{(K)}\le X_i^-,
\]

we have

\[
X_i
=
X_i^+-X_i^-
\le
X_i^+-Y_i^{(K)}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{S_n}{n}
\le
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^+
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i^{(K)}.
\]

Taking the limit superior as \(n\to\infty\), for every fixed \(K\),

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n}
\le
\mu^+-\mu_K
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Now,

\[
Y_1^{(K)}\uparrow X_1^-
\qquad\text{as }K\to\infty.
\]

By the monotone convergence theorem,

\[
\mu_K
=
E(Y_1^{(K)})
\uparrow
E(X_1^-)
=
\infty.
\]

Fix \(A>0\). We can choose \(K\) sufficiently large so that

\[
\mu_K-\mu^+>A.
\]

For this \(K\),

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n}
\le
\mu^+-\mu_K
<
-A
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Since \(A>0\) is arbitrary,

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{n}
=
-\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\frac{S_n}{n}\to-\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

### Ex 39

::: problem
If \(\{A_n,n\ge1\}\) are independent events, show that

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1_{A_i}
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nP(A_i)
\xrightarrow{P}0.
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
X_n=1_{A_n}.
\]

Since \(\{A_n\}\) are independent, \(\{X_n\}\) are independent. Also,

\[
E(X_n)=P(A_n),
\]

and

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)
&=
E(X_n^2)-E(X_n)^2\\
&=
P(A_n)-P(A_n)^2\\
&\le1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.
\]

By independence,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(S_n)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)
\le n.
\]

Therefore, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), by Chebyshev's inequality,

\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(
\left|
\frac{S_n-E(S_n)}n
\right|>\varepsilon
\right)
&\le
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}
{n^2\varepsilon^2}\\
&\le
\frac1{n\varepsilon^2}
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n1_{A_i}
\]

and

\[
E(S_n)=\sum_{i=1}^nP(A_i),
\]

we have

\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1_{A_i}
-
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nP(A_i)
\xrightarrow{P}0.
\]


### Ex 43

::: problem
(a) Fix a real number \(p\in(0,1)\) and let \(\{B_n,n\ge1\}\) be iid Bernoulli random variables with

\[
P[B_n=1]=p=1-P[B_n=0].
\]

Define

\[
Y=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{B_n}{2^n}.
\]

Verify that the series converges. What is the range of \(Y\)? What is the mean and variance of \(Y\)? Let \(Q_p\) be the distribution of \(Y\). Where does \(Q_p\) concentrate?

Use the SLLN to show that if \(p\ne p'\), then \(Q_p\) and \(Q_{p'}\) are mutually singular; that is, there exists a set \(A\) such that \(Q_p(A)=1\) and \(Q_{p'}(A)=0\).

(b) Let \(F_p(x)\) be the distribution function corresponding to \(Q_p\). Show \(F_p(x)\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,1]\), \(F_p(0)=0\), \(F_p(1)=1\), and satisfies

\[
F_p(x)
=
\begin{cases}
(1-p)F_p(2x), & 0\le x\le \frac12,\\[4pt]
1-p+pF_p(2x-1), & \frac12\le x\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

#### (a)

Let

\[
Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{B_i}{2^i}.
\]

For \(n>m\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
|Y_n-Y_m|
&=
\left|
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\frac{B_i}{2^i}
\right|\\
&\le
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\frac1{2^i}
\longrightarrow0
\end{aligned}
\]

as \(m,n\to\infty\). Therefore, \(\{Y_n\}\) is Cauchy and the series converges for every outcome.

Since \(Y\) is the undetermined binary form of a number in \([0,1]\), its range is \([0,1]\).

Furthermore, since \(0\le Y_n\le1\) and \(Y_n\to Y\), by the dominated convergence theorem,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E(Y)
&=
\lim_{n\to\infty}E(Y_n)\\
&=
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{E(B_i)}{2^i}\\
&=
p\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac1{2^i}\\
&=
p.
\end{aligned}
\]

Also, by independence,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(B_i)}{2^{2i}}\\
&=
p(1-p)
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac1{4^i}\\
&=
\frac13p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(x\in[0,1]\), let \(d_i(x)\) denote the \(i\)-th digit in its canonical binary expansion, and define

\[
A_p
=
\left\{
x\in[0,1]:
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nd_i(x)\to p
\right\}.
\]

Apart from the binary-expansion ambiguity at dyadic rationals, which has probability zero,

\[
d_i(Y)=B_i.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_p(A_p)
&=
P_p(Y\in A_p)\\
&=
P_p\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nB_i\to p
\right)\\
&=
1
\end{aligned}
\]

by the SLLN. Thus, \(Q_p\) concentrates on \(A_p\).

Now let \(p'\ne p\). Similarly,

\[
Q_{p'}(A_{p'})=1.
\]

By the uniqueness of limits,

\[
A_p\cap A_{p'}=\varnothing.
\]

Therefore,

\[
Q_{p'}(A_p)=0,
\]

while

\[
Q_p(A_p)=1.
\]

Hence, \(Q_p\) and \(Q_{p'}\) are mutually singular.

#### (b)

First, we show that \(F_p\) is strictly increasing.

Let \(0\le x<y\le1\). There exists a finite binary cylinder interval contained in \((x,y)\). Suppose its fixed binary prefix contains \(r_1\) digits equal to \(1\) and \(r_0\) digits equal to \(0\). Its \(Q_p\)-probability is

\[
p^{r_1}(1-p)^{r_0}>0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
F_p(y)-F_p(x)
=
Q_p((x,y])
>
0.
\]

Thus, \(F_p\) is strictly increasing on \([0,1]\).

Next, we show that \(F_p\) is continuous. Let

\[
a=\max\{p,1-p\}<1.
\]

For any fixed \(x\in[0,1]\), the event \(\{Y=x\}\) determines the first \(n\) binary digits of \(Y\), with at most two possible prefixes because a dyadic rational may have two binary expansions. Hence,

\[
Q_p(\{x\})
\le
2a^n.
\]

Letting \(n\to\infty\),

\[
Q_p(\{x\})=0.
\]

Thus, \(Q_p\) has no atoms, and consequently \(F_p\) is continuous.

For the endpoints,

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_p(0)
&=
P(Y=0)\\
&=
P(B_i=0\text{ for every }i)\\
&=
\lim_{n\to\infty}(1-p)^n\\
&=
0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Also, since \(0\le Y\le1\),

\[
F_p(1)=P(Y\le1)=1.
\]

Lastly, define

\[
Y'
=
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{B_n}{2^{n-1}}.
\]

Then \(Y'\) is independent of \(B_1\), has the same distribution as \(Y\), and

\[
Y=\frac{B_1+Y'}2.
\]

For \(0\le x\le\frac12\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_p(x)
&=
P(Y\le x)\\
&=
P(B_1=0,\ Y'\le2x)\\
&=
P(B_1=0)P(Y'\le2x)\\
&=
(1-p)F_p(2x).
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(\frac12\le x\le1\), if \(B_1=0\), then \(Y\le\frac12\le x\). If \(B_1=1\), then

\[
Y\le x
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Y'\le2x-1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_p(x)
&=
P(B_1=0)
+
P(B_1=1,\ Y'\le2x-1)\\
&=
1-p+pF_p(2x-1).
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
F_p(x)
=
\begin{cases}
(1-p)F_p(2x), & 0\le x\le \frac12,\\[4pt]
1-p+pF_p(2x-1), & \frac12\le x\le1.
\end{cases}
}
\]

### Ex 44

::: problem
Let \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) be iid with values in the set \(S=\{1,\ldots,17\}\). Define the (discrete) density

\[
f_0(y)=P[X_1=y],
\qquad y\in S.
\]

Let \(f_1\ne f_0\) be another probability mass function on \(S\) so that for \(y\in S\), we have \(f_1(y)\ge0\) and

\[
\sum_{j\in S}f_1(j)=1.
\]

Set

\[
Z_n=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{f_1(X_i)}{f_0(X_i)},
\qquad n\ge1.
\]

Prove that

\[
Z_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}0.
\]

(Consider \(Y_n=\log Z_n\).)
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
W_n=\frac{f_1(X_n)}{f_0(X_n)}
\]

and define

\[
S_0=\{j\in S:f_0(j)>0\}.
\]

Since \(X_n\) has probability mass function \(f_0\),

\[
P(X_n\in S_0)=1.
\]

We consider two cases.

First, suppose that there exists \(j\in S_0\) such that

\[
f_1(j)=0.
\]

For this particular \(j\),

\[
P(X_n=j)=f_0(j)>0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(X_n=j)=\infty.
\]

Since the events \(\{X_n=j\}\) are independent, by Borel--Cantelli,

\[
P(X_n=j\text{ i.o.})=1.
\]

When \(X_n=j\),

\[
W_n=\frac{f_1(j)}{f_0(j)}=0.
\]

Thus, almost surely, one of the factors in

\[
Z_n=\prod_{i=1}^nW_i
\]

eventually equals \(0\), and \(Z_n\) remains \(0\) afterward. Therefore,

\[
Z_n\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Now suppose that

\[
f_1(j)>0
\qquad\text{for every }j\in S_0.
\]

Then \(\log W_n\) is finite almost surely. Since the \(X_n\)'s are iid, the random variables \(\{\log W_n\}\) are also iid. Because \(S\) is finite,

\[
E_{f_0}|\log W_1|<\infty.
\]

We have

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{f_0}(\log W_1)
&=
\sum_{j\in S_0}
f_0(j)
\log\frac{f_1(j)}{f_0(j)}\\
&\le
\log\left(
\sum_{j\in S_0}
f_0(j)\frac{f_1(j)}{f_0(j)}
\right)\\
&=
\log\left(
\sum_{j\in S_0}f_1(j)
\right)\\
&\le
\log 1\\
&=
0,
\end{aligned}
\]

where the first inequality follows from Jensen's inequality.

We claim that the inequality is strict. If equality held, then we would need

\[
\sum_{j\in S_0}f_1(j)=1,
\]

so \(f_1\) would have no mass outside \(S_0\). Also, equality in Jensen's inequality would imply that there exists a constant \(c\) such that

\[
\frac{f_1(j)}{f_0(j)}=c
\qquad\text{for every }j\in S_0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
1
=
\sum_{j\in S_0}f_1(j)
=
c\sum_{j\in S_0}f_0(j)
=
c.
\]

Hence \(c=1\), so

\[
f_1(j)=f_0(j)
\qquad\text{for every }j\in S_0.
\]

Together with the fact that \(f_1\) has no mass outside \(S_0\), this would imply

\[
f_1=f_0,
\]

which contradicts the assumption. Thus,

\[
E_{f_0}(\log W_1)<0.
\]

Now,

\[
\log Z_n
=
\log\left(
\prod_{i=1}^nW_i
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n\log W_i.
\]

By the SLLN,

\[
\frac1n\log Z_n
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log W_i
\to
E_{f_0}(\log W_1)
<0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Let

\[
\mu=E_{f_0}(\log W_1)<0.
\]

Almost surely, for sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
\frac1n\log Z_n<\frac{\mu}{2}<0.
\]

Hence,

\[
\log Z_n<\frac{\mu n}{2}\to-\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
Z_n\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

### Ex 45

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) are iid random variables taking values in the alphabet

\[
S=\{1,\ldots,r\}
\]

with positive probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_r\). Define

\[
p_n(i_1,\ldots,i_n)
=
P[X_1=i_1,\ldots,X_n=i_n],
\]

and set

\[
\chi_n(\omega)
:=
p_n\bigl(X_1(\omega),\ldots,X_n(\omega)\bigr).
\]

Then \(\chi_n(\omega)\) is the probability that in a new sample of \(n\) observations, what is observed matches the original observations. Show that

\[
-\frac1n\log\chi_n(\omega)
\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}
H
:=
-\sum_{i=1}^r p_i\log p_i.
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Since \(\{X_n\}\) are iid, for any \(i_1,\ldots,i_n\in S\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_n(i_1,\ldots,i_n)
&=
P(X_1=i_1,\ldots,X_n=i_n)\\
&=
P(X_1=i_1)\cdots P(X_n=i_n)\\
&=
p_{i_1}\cdots p_{i_n}\\
&=
\prod_{k=1}^n p_{i_k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi_n(\omega)
&=
p_n\bigl(X_1(\omega),\ldots,X_n(\omega)\bigr)\\
&=
\prod_{k=1}^n p_{X_k(\omega)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Taking logarithms,

\[
\log\chi_n(\omega)
=
\sum_{k=1}^n\log p_{X_k(\omega)}.
\]

Let

\[
Y_k=-\log p_{X_k}.
\]

Since the \(X_k\)'s are iid, the \(Y_k\)'s are also iid. Moreover, because the alphabet is finite and \(p_j>0\) for every \(j\),

\[
E|Y_1|<\infty.
\]

We have

\[
\begin{aligned}
E(Y_1)
&=
E\left(-\log p_{X_1}\right)\\
&=
-\sum_{j=1}^r
P(X_1=j)\log p_j\\
&=
-\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\log p_j\\
&=
H.
\end{aligned}
\]

By the SLLN,

\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nY_k
\longrightarrow H
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Finally,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^nY_k
&=
-\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\log p_{X_k}\\
&=
-\frac1n\log\left(\prod_{k=1}^np_{X_k}\right)\\
&=
-\frac1n\log\chi_n.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
-\frac1n\log\chi_n(\omega)
\longrightarrow
H
=
-\sum_{j=1}^rp_j\log p_j
\qquad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

### Ex 6

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_k,k\ge1\}\) are independent random variables and suppose \(X_k\) has a gamma density \(f_k(x)\)

\[
f_k(x)
=
\frac{x^{\gamma_k-1}e^{-x}}
{\Gamma(\gamma_k)},
\qquad
x>0,\ \gamma_k>0.
\]

Give necessary and sufficient conditions for

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k
\]

to converge almost surely. (Compare with the treatment of sums of exponentially distributed random variables.)
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

We claim that

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k
\]

converges almost surely if and only if

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k<\infty.
\]

Since

\[
X_k\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\gamma_k,1),
\]

we have

\[
E(X_k)=\gamma_k,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_k)=\gamma_k.
\]

"$\Leftarrow$"

Suppose

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k<\infty.
\]

Since \(X_k\ge0\), by Tonelli's theorem,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k\right)
&=
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}E(X_k)\\
&=
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k\\
&<
\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k<\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

"$\Rightarrow$"

Suppose

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k
\]

converges almost surely. We show that necessarily

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k<\infty.
\]

Suppose, to the contrary, that

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k=\infty.
\]

Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k
\]

and

\[
a_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\gamma_k.
\]

Then

\[
a_n\to\infty.
\]

Also, by independence,

\[
E(S_n)=a_n
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(S_n)
=
\sum_{k=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_k)
=
a_n.
\]

By Chebyshev's inequality,

\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(S_n\le\frac{a_n}{2}\right)
&\le
P\left(
|S_n-E(S_n)|
\ge
\frac{a_n}{2}
\right)\\
&\le
\frac{4\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}{a_n^2}\\
&=
\frac4{a_n}\\
&\to0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now fix \(M>0\). Since \(a_n\to\infty\), for sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
M\le\frac{a_n}{2}.
\]

Hence,

\[
P(S_n\le M)
\le
P\left(S_n\le\frac{a_n}{2}\right)
\to0.
\]

Since \(X_k\ge0\), the sequence \(S_n\) is increasing. Therefore,

\[
\{S_n\le M\}
\downarrow
\left\{
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k\le M
\right\}.
\]

By continuity of probability from above,

\[
P\left(
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k\le M
\right)
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(S_n\le M)
=
0.
\]

This is true for every \(M\in\mathbb N\). Thus,

\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k<\infty
\right)
&=
P\left(
\bigcup_{M=1}^{\infty}
\left\{
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k\le M
\right\}
\right)\\
&=
0.
\end{aligned}
\]

This contradicts the assumption that the series converges almost surely.

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k<\infty.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}X_k
\text{ converges a.s.}
\iff
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k<\infty.
}
\]

### Ex 11

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) are iid with a symmetric distribution. Then

\[
\sum_n \frac{X_n}{n}
\]

converges almost surely iff \(E(|X_1|)<\infty\).
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

First suppose

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{X_n}{n}
\]

converges almost surely. Then necessarily

\[
\frac{X_n}{n}\to0
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

Therefore, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
P\left(
\left|\frac{X_n}{n}\right|>\varepsilon
\text{ i.o.}
\right)
=
0.
\]

Since the \(X_n\)'s are independent, the events

\[
\{|X_n|>\varepsilon n\}
\]

are independent. Hence, by the converse part of Borel--Cantelli,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon n)
<
\infty.
\]

Taking \(\varepsilon=1\), and using that the \(X_n\)'s are identically distributed,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
P(|X_1|>n)
<
\infty.
\]

Also,

\[
E|X_1|
=
\int_0^\infty P(|X_1|>t)\,dt.
\]

Since \(P(|X_1|>t)\) is decreasing,

\[
E|X_1|
\le
P(|X_1|>0)
+
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(|X_1|>n)
<
\infty.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{X_n}{n}
\text{ converges a.s.}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E|X_1|<\infty.
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
E|X_1|<\infty.
\]

Since the distribution of \(X_1\) is symmetric,

\[
E(X_1)=0.
\]

Let

\[
Y_n=\frac{X_n}{n}.
\]

We apply the three-series theorem with truncation level \(c=1\).

First,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(|Y_n|>1)
&=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(|X_n|>n)\\
&=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(|X_1|>n)\\
&<
\infty,
\end{aligned}
\]

since \(E|X_1|<\infty\).

Second, by symmetry,

\[
E\left[
Y_n1_{\{|Y_n|\le1\}}
\right]
=
\frac1n
E\left[
X_n1_{\{|X_n|\le n\}}
\right]
=
0.
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
E\left[
Y_n1_{\{|Y_n|\le1\}}
\right]
=
0.
\]

Finally, since the truncated variable is still symmetric,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\left(
Y_n1_{\{|Y_n|\le1\}}
\right)
&=
E\left[
Y_n^2 1_{\{|Y_n|\le1\}}
\right]\\
&=
\frac1{n^2}
E\left[
X_n^2 1_{\{|X_n|\le n\}}
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\operatorname{Var}\left(
Y_n1_{\{|Y_n|\le1\}}
\right)
&=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\frac1{n^2}
E\left[
X_1^2 1_{\{|X_1|\le n\}}
\right]\\
&=
E\left[
X_1^2
\sum_{n\ge |X_1|}
\frac1{n^2}
\right],
\end{aligned}
\]

where the last equality follows from Tonelli's theorem.

Now isolate the inner sum. For \(x\ge1\), letting \(m=\lceil x\rceil\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n\ge x}\frac1{n^2}
&=
\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}\\
&\le
\frac1{m^2}
+
\int_m^\infty\frac1{t^2}\,dt\\
&\le
\frac2x.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(0\le x<1\),

\[
x^2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}
\le
\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}\right)x.
\]

Thus there exists a finite constant \(C\) such that

\[
x^2\sum_{n\ge x}\frac1{n^2}
\le
Cx,
\qquad x\ge0.
\]

Hence,

\[
E\left[
X_1^2
\sum_{n\ge |X_1|}
\frac1{n^2}
\right]
\le
C E|X_1|
<
\infty.
\]

Therefore all three conditions of the three-series theorem hold, and

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{X_n}{n}
\]

converges almost surely.

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{X_n}{n}
\text{ converges a.s.}
\iff
E|X_1|<\infty.
}
\]


$\textbf{Note:}$ We should note that in this exercise, symmetric means symmetric about \(0\). If the distribution is instead symmetric about some \(c\neq0\), then the series will not converge.


### Ex 13

::: problem
Use the three series theorem to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for \(\sum_n X_n\) to converge a.s. when \(\{X_n\}\) are independent and exponentially distributed.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
X_n\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_n),
\]

where \(\lambda_n>0\) is the rate parameter. Then

\[
E(X_n)=\frac1{\lambda_n},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=\frac1{\lambda_n^2}.
\]

We claim that

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\]

converges almost surely if and only if

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}<\infty.
\]

Fix \(c>0\). Since \(X_n\ge0\), the three series theorem requires us to consider

\[
\sum_nP(X_n>c),
\]

\[
\sum_n
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right),
\]

and

\[
\sum_n
\operatorname{Var}\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right).
\]

* \((\Rightarrow)\)

Suppose

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\]

converges almost surely.

By the three series theorem,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(X_n>c)<\infty.
\]

Since \(X_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_n)\),

\[
P(X_n>c)=e^{-c\lambda_n}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-c\lambda_n}<\infty.
\]

In particular,

\[
e^{-c\lambda_n}\to0,
\]

so

\[
\lambda_n\to\infty.
\]

Also, the three series theorem gives

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right)
<
\infty.
\]

For each \(n\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right)
&=
\int_0^c x\lambda_ne^{-\lambda_nx}\,dx\\
&=
\frac{1-(1+c\lambda_n)e^{-c\lambda_n}}
{\lambda_n}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\lambda_n\to\infty\),

\[
(1+c\lambda_n)e^{-c\lambda_n}\to0.
\]

Hence, for sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
1-(1+c\lambda_n)e^{-c\lambda_n}
\ge\frac12.
\]

Therefore,

\[
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right)
\ge
\frac1{2\lambda_n}
\]

eventually. Thus,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}
<
\infty.
\]

* \((\Leftarrow)\)

Conversely, suppose

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}<\infty.
\]

We verify the three conditions of the three series theorem.

First,

\[
P(X_n>c)=e^{-c\lambda_n}.
\]

To control this series, consider

\[
f(x)=xe^{-cx},
\qquad x>0.
\]

Then

\[
f'(x)=e^{-cx}(1-cx).
\]

Thus \(f\) reaches its maximum at

\[
x=\frac1c,
\]

and

\[
f\left(\frac1c\right)=\frac1{ce}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
xe^{-cx}\le\frac1{ce},
\]

so

\[
e^{-cx}\le\frac1{ce}\frac1x.
\]

Taking \(x=\lambda_n\),

\[
e^{-c\lambda_n}
\le
\frac1{ce}\frac1{\lambda_n}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}P(X_n>c)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}e^{-c\lambda_n}
\le
\frac1{ce}
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}
<
\infty.
\]

Second,

\[
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right)
\le
E(X_n)
=
\frac1{\lambda_n}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}\right)
<
\infty.
\]

Finally,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\left(
X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}
\right)
&\le
E\left(
X_n^2 1_{\{X_n\le c\}}
\right)\\
&\le
E(X_n^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

For an exponential random variable,

\[
E(X_n^2)
=
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)+E(X_n)^2
=
\frac2{\lambda_n^2}.
\]

Since

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}<\infty,
\]

we have \(\lambda_n\to\infty\), so eventually \(\lambda_n\ge1\), and therefore

\[
\frac1{\lambda_n^2}
\le
\frac1{\lambda_n}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\operatorname{Var}\left(
X_n1_{\{X_n\le c\}}
\right)
\le
2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n^2}
<
\infty.
\]

Thus all three conditions of the three series theorem hold, and

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\]

converges almost surely.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\text{ converges a.s.}
\iff
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{\lambda_n}<\infty.
}
\]


### Ex 14

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) are independent, normally distributed with

\[
E(X_n)=\mu_n,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=\sigma_n^2.
\]

Show that \(\sum_n X_n\) converges almost surely iff \(\sum_n\mu_n\) converges and $\sum_n\sigma_n^2<\infty$.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

First suppose

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\]

converges almost surely. Let

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.
\]

Then \(\{S_n\}\) is Cauchy in probability. For \(m<n\), define

\[
Z_{m,n}=S_n-S_m
=
\sum_{i=m+1}^nX_i.
\]

Thus,

\[
Z_{m,n}\xrightarrow{P}0
\qquad\text{as }m,n\to\infty.
\]

Since the \(X_i\)'s are independent and normally distributed,

\[
Z_{m,n}
\sim
N\left(
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\mu_i,
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\sigma_i^2
\right).
\]

Let

\[
a_{m,n}
=
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\mu_i,
\qquad
b_{m,n}
=
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\sigma_i^2.
\]

We first show that

\[
b_{m,n}\to0.
\]

Suppose not. Then there exists \(\delta>0\) and arbitrarily large \(m<n\) such that

\[
b_{m,n}\ge\delta.
\]

The density \(f_{m,n}\) of \(Z_{m,n}\) satisfies

\[
f_{m,n}(x)
\le
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi b_{m,n}}}
\le
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\delta}}.
\]

Therefore, for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(|Z_{m,n}|\le\varepsilon)
&=
\int_{-\varepsilon}^{\varepsilon}
f_{m,n}(x)\,dx\\
&\le
\frac{2\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) such that

\[
\frac{2\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi\delta}}<1.
\]

This contradicts

\[
Z_{m,n}\xrightarrow{P}0,
\]

which requires

\[
P(|Z_{m,n}|\le\varepsilon)\to1.
\]

Hence,

\[
b_{m,n}
=
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\sigma_i^2
\to0.
\]

Therefore the partial sums of

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma_n^2
\]

are Cauchy. Since the terms are nonnegative,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma_n^2<\infty.
\]

Next, by Chebyshev's inequality,

\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(
|Z_{m,n}-a_{m,n}|>\varepsilon
\right)
&\le
\frac{b_{m,n}}{\varepsilon^2}\\
&\to0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus,

\[
Z_{m,n}-a_{m,n}\xrightarrow{P}0.
\]

Since also

\[
Z_{m,n}\xrightarrow{P}0,
\]

we have

\[
a_{m,n}
=
Z_{m,n}-(Z_{m,n}-a_{m,n})
\xrightarrow{P}0.
\]

Since \(a_{m,n}\) is deterministic,

\[
a_{m,n}\to0.
\]

That is,

\[
\sum_{i=m+1}^n\mu_i\to0
\qquad\text{as }m,n\to\infty.
\]

By the Cauchy criterion,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n
\]

converges.

Conversely, suppose

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n
\]

converges and

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma_n^2<\infty.
\]

Write

\[
X_n=(X_n-\mu_n)+\mu_n.
\]

The random variables \(\{X_n-\mu_n\}\) are independent and satisfy

\[
E(X_n-\mu_n)=0
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_n-\mu_n)
=
\sigma_n^2.
\]

Since

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\operatorname{Var}(X_n-\mu_n)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma_n^2
<
\infty,
\]

the Kolmogorov convergence criterion gives

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(X_n-\mu_n)
\]

converges almost surely.

Since

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n
\]

also converges,

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(X_n-\mu_n)
+
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n
\]

converges almost surely.

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}X_n
\text{ converges a.s.}
\iff
\left[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu_n
\text{ converges}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sigma_n^2<\infty
\right].
}
\]

### Ex 15

::: problem
Prove the three series theorem reduces to a two series theorem when the
random variables are positive. If \(V_n\ge0\) are independent, then
\(\sum_n V_n<\infty\) a.s. iff for any \(c>0\), we have

\[
\sum_nP[V_n>c]<\infty,
\tag{i}
\]

\[
\sum_nE(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})<\infty.
\tag{ii}
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Suppose first that

\[
\sum_nV_n<\infty
\]

almost surely. By the Kolmogorov three series theorem, for any \(c>0\),

\[
\sum_nP(V_n>c)<\infty
\]

and

\[
\sum_nE(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})
\]

converges. Since \(V_n\ge0\),

\[
E(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})\ge0,
\]

so

\[
\sum_nE(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})<\infty.
\]

Conversely, suppose for some \(c>0\),

\[
\sum_nP(V_n>c)<\infty
\]

and

\[
\sum_nE(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})<\infty.
\]

Let

\[
V_n'=V_n1_{[V_n\le c]}.
\]

Then

\[
\sum_nP(V_n'\ne V_n)
=
\sum_nP(V_n>c)
<
\infty.
\]

By Borel--Cantelli,

\[
P(V_n'\ne V_n\text{ i.o.})=0,
\]

so \(\{V_n'\}\) and \(\{V_n\}\) are tail equivalent.

For \(\sum_nV_n'\), since \(V_n'\ge0\), by Tonelli,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left(\sum_nV_n'\right)
&=
\sum_nE(V_n')\\
&=
\sum_nE(V_n1_{[V_n\le c]})\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nV_n'<\infty
\]

almost surely.

Since \(\{V_n'\}\) and \(\{V_n\}\) are tail equivalent,

\[
\sum_nV_n<\infty
\]

almost surely.

Thus, for non-negative independent random variables, the variance series in
the three series theorem is redundant.


### Ex 17

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n\}\) are independent with

\[
P[X_k=k^2]=\frac1{k^2},
\qquad
P[X_k=-1]=1-\frac1{k^2}.
\]

Prove

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i
\]

exists a.s. and find the limit.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Let

\[
Y_k=-1
\]

with probability \(1\). Then

\[
P(Y_k\ne X_k)
=
P(X_k=k^2)
=
\frac1{k^2}.
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_kP(Y_k\ne X_k)
=
\sum_k\frac1{k^2}
<
\infty.
\]

By Borel--Cantelli,

\[
P(Y_k\ne X_k\text{ i.o.})=0.
\]

Thus \(\{Y_k\}\) and \(\{X_k\}\) are tail equivalent. In particular, almost surely
there exists a finite \(N\) such that

\[
X_k=Y_k=-1,
\qquad k\ge N.
\]

Therefore, for sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
\sum_{k=1}^nX_k
=
\sum_{k=1}^nY_k+C
\]

for some finite random constant \(C\).

But

\[
\sum_{k=1}^nY_k=-n\to-\infty.
\]

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k=-\infty
}
\]

almost surely.

### Ex 19

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n, n\ge 1\}\) are non-negative independent random variables. Then
\(\sum_n X_n<\infty\) almost surely iff

\[
\sum_n E\left(\frac{X_n}{1+X_n}\right)<\infty
\]

iff

\[
\sum_n E(X_n\wedge1)<\infty.
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Denote

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a)&\quad \sum_n X_n<\infty \quad\text{a.s.},\\
(b)&\quad \sum_nE\left(\frac{X_n}{1+X_n}\right)<\infty,\\
(c)&\quad \sum_nE(X_n\wedge1)<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(x\ge0\),

\[
\frac{x}{1+x}
\le
x\wedge1
\le
2\frac{x}{1+x}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
(b)\iff(c).
\]

Now suppose \((b)\) holds. Since \((b)\Rightarrow(c)\),

\[
\sum_nE(X_n\wedge1)<\infty.
\]

For \(c=1\),

\[
X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}
\le
X_n\wedge1,
\]

so

\[
\sum_nE\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}\right)
\le
\sum_nE(X_n\wedge1)
<
\infty.
\]

Also,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left(\frac{X_n}{1+X_n}\right)
&\ge
E\left(
\frac{X_n}{1+X_n}1_{\{X_n>1\}}
\right)\\
&\ge
\frac12P(X_n>1).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_nP(X_n>1)
\le
2\sum_nE\left(\frac{X_n}{1+X_n}\right)
<
\infty.
\]

Thus, by the result of Ex 15,

\[
\sum_nX_n<\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

and therefore

\[
(b)\Rightarrow(a).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
\sum_nX_n<\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

By Ex 15, with \(c=1\),

\[
\sum_nE\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}\right)<\infty
\]

and

\[
\sum_nP(X_n>1)<\infty.
\]

Since

\[
X_n\wedge1
=
X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}
+
1_{\{X_n>1\}},
\]

we have

\[
E(X_n\wedge1)
=
E\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}\right)
+
P(X_n>1).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_nE(X_n\wedge1)
&=
\sum_nE\left(X_n1_{\{X_n\le1\}}\right)
+
\sum_nP(X_n>1)\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus,

\[
(a)\Rightarrow(c).
\]

Together with \((b)\iff(c)\), we obtain

\[
\boxed{(a)\iff(b)\iff(c)}.
\]

### Ex 20

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) are independent random variables with \(E(X_n)=0\)
for all \(n\). If

\[
\sum_n E\left(
X_n^2 1_{[|X_n|\le1]}
+
|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}
\right)<\infty,
\]

then \(\sum_nX_n\) converges almost surely.

Hint: We have

\[
0=E(X_n)
=
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|\le1]})
+
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|>1]}).
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

What we have is

\[
\sum_n
E\left(
X_n^2 1_{[|X_n|\le1]}
+
|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}
\right)
<\infty.
\]

That is,

\[
\sum_nE\left(X_n^2 1_{[|X_n|\le1]}\right)
+
\sum_nE\left(|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}\right)
<\infty.
\]

Since both terms are non-negative series, we have

\[
\sum_nE\left(X_n^2 1_{[|X_n|\le1]}\right)<\infty
\]

and

\[
\sum_nE\left(|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}\right)<\infty.
\]

Firstly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
E\left(|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}\right)
&=
\int_\Omega |X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}\,dP\\
&\ge
\int_\Omega 1_{[|X_n|>1]}\,dP\\
&=
P(|X_n|>1).
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nP(|X_n|>1)
\le
\sum_nE\left(|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}\right)
<\infty.
\]

Secondly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_n
\operatorname{Var}\left(
X_n1_{[|X_n|\le1]}
\right)
&\le
\sum_n
E\left(
X_n^2 1_{[|X_n|\le1]}
\right)\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]

Lastly, since \(E(X_n)=0\),

\[
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|\le1]})
=
-
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|>1]}).
\]

Also,

\[
\left|
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|>1]})
\right|
\le
E\left(
|X_n|1_{[|X_n|>1]}
\right).
\]

Hence,

\[
\sum_n
\left|
E(X_n1_{[|X_n|>1]})
\right|
<\infty.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nE(X_n1_{[|X_n|\le1]})
\]

converges.

Thus all three conditions of the Kolmogorov three series theorem hold for
\(c=1\), and hence

\[
\boxed{
\sum_nX_n\text{ converges a.s.}
}
\]

### Ex 26

::: problem
If \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) is defined as in the St. Petersburg paradox of Problem 24,
show almost surely that

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty,
\]

so that for the partial sums we also have almost surely

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{S_n}{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty.
\]

Thus we have another example of a sequence converging in probability but
not almost surely.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

In the St. Petersburg paradox, \(\{X_n\}\) are iid and

\[
P(X_1=2^k)=2^{-k},
\qquad k\ge1.
\]

Thus,

\[
P(X_1>2^m)
=
\sum_{k=m+1}^{\infty}2^{-k}
=
2^{-m}.
\]

To show

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty
\]

almost surely, it is enough to show that for every \(M>0\),

\[
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}>M
\]

happens infinitely often almost surely.

Fix \(M>0\). Consider

\[
P(X_n>M n\log_2 n).
\]

Let \(j\) be such that

\[
2^j
\le
M n\log_2 n
<
2^{j+1}.
\]

Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_n>M n\log_2 n)
&=
P(X_n\ge2^{j+1})\\
&=
\sum_{k=j+1}^{\infty}2^{-k}\\
&=
2^{-j}\\
&\ge
\frac{1}{M n\log_2 n}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nP(X_n>M n\log_2 n)
\ge
\frac1M
\sum_n\frac1{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty.
\]

Since the \(X_n\)'s are independent, by Borel--Cantelli,

\[
P\left(
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}>M
\text{ i.o.}
\right)
=
1.
\]

Now take \(M=1,2,\ldots\). Since a countable intersection of probability-one
events still has probability one,

\[
P\left(
\bigcap_{M=1}^{\infty}
\left\{
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}>M
\text{ i.o.}
\right\}
\right)
=
1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty
\quad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

For

\[
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,
\]

since \(X_i\ge0\),

\[
S_n\ge X_n.
\]

Hence,

\[
\frac{S_n}{n\log_2 n}
\ge
\frac{X_n}{n\log_2 n},
\]

and consequently,

\[
\boxed{
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\frac{S_n}{n\log_2 n}
=
\infty
\quad\text{a.s.}
}
\]

From Problem 24,

\[
\frac{S_n}{n\log_2 n}
\xrightarrow{P}1,
\]

so this gives an example of convergence in probability without almost sure
convergence.

### Ex 33

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_j,j\ge1\}\) are independent with

\[
P[X_n=n^{-\alpha}]
=
P[X_n=-n^{-\alpha}]
=
\frac12.
\]

Use the Kolmogorov convergence criterion to verify that if \(\alpha>1/2\), then
\(\sum_nX_n\) converges almost surely. Use the Kolmogorov three series theorem
to verify that \(\alpha>1/2\) is necessary for convergence. Verify that

\[
\sum_nE(|X_n|)<\infty
\]

iff \(\alpha>1\).
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Since

\[
E(X_n)
=
\frac12n^{-\alpha}
-
\frac12n^{-\alpha}
=
0,
\]

we have

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_n)
=
E(X_n^2)
=
\frac1{n^{2\alpha}}.
\]

When

\[
\alpha>\frac12,
\]

\[
\sum_n\operatorname{Var}(X_n)
=
\sum_n\frac1{n^{2\alpha}}
<
\infty.
\]

Therefore, by the Kolmogorov convergence criterion,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_nX_n\text{ converges a.s.}
}
\]

when \(\alpha>1/2\).

Now consider necessity using the Kolmogorov three series theorem.

First suppose \(\alpha\ge0\), and take \(c=1\). Since

\[
|X_n|=n^{-\alpha}\le1,
\]

we have

\[
\sum_nP(|X_n|>1)=0.
\]

Also,

\[
\sum_nE\left(X_n1_{\{|X_n|\le1\}}\right)
=
\sum_nE(X_n)
=
0.
\]

For the variance series,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_n
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
X_n1_{\{|X_n|\le1\}}
\right)
&=
\sum_n\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\\
&=
\sum_n\frac1{n^{2\alpha}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

This series converges iff

\[
2\alpha>1,
\]

that is,

\[
\alpha>\frac12.
\]

Thus, for \(0\le\alpha\le1/2\), the third condition of the three series theorem
fails, so \(\sum_nX_n\) cannot converge almost surely.

When \(\alpha<0\), for any constant \(c>0\),

\[
n^{-\alpha}\to\infty.
\]

Hence, for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
n^{-\alpha}>c.
\]

Since

\[
|X_n|=n^{-\alpha}
\]

with probability \(1\), we have eventually

\[
P(|X_n|>c)=1.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nP(|X_n|>c)=\infty,
\]

so the first condition of the three series theorem fails.

Hence,

\[
\boxed{
\sum_nX_n\text{ converges a.s.}
\iff
\alpha>\frac12.
}
\]

Finally,

\[
E(|X_n|)
=
\frac1{n^\alpha}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sum_nE(|X_n|)
=
\sum_n\frac1{n^\alpha}
<
\infty
\]

iff

\[
\boxed{\alpha>1}.
\]

### Ex 36

::: problem
Suppose \(\{X_n,n\ge1\}\) is independent and \(X_k\ge0\). If for some
\(\delta\in(0,1)\) there exists \(x\) such that for all \(k\)

\[
\int_{[X_k>x]}X_k\,dP
\le
\delta E(X_k),
\]

then almost sure convergence of \(\sum_nX_n\) implies $\sum_nE(X_n)<\infty$ as well.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

From

\[
\int_{[X_k>x]}X_k\,dP
\le
\delta E(X_k),
\]

we have

\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X_k)
&=
\int_{[X_k\le x]}X_k\,dP
+
\int_{[X_k>x]}X_k\,dP.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\int_{[X_k\le x]}X_k\,dP
\ge
(1-\delta)E(X_k).
\]

Now suppose

\[
\sum_nX_n<\infty
\qquad\text{a.s.}
\]

By the necessity part of Kolmogorov's three series theorem,

\[
\sum_n
E\left(
X_n1_{[X_n\le x]}
\right)
<\infty.
\]

But

\[
E\left(
X_n1_{[X_n\le x]}
\right)
=
\int_{[X_n\le x]}X_n\,dP
\ge
(1-\delta)E(X_n).
\]

Hence,

\[
(1-\delta)\sum_nE(X_n)
\le
\sum_n
E\left(
X_n1_{[X_n\le x]}
\right)
<
\infty.
\]

Since \(1-\delta>0\),

\[
\boxed{
\sum_nE(X_n)<\infty.
}
\]

### Ex 37

$\textbf{Note:}$

Ex 37 is essentially a repetition of Ex 13. Both exercises ask for the necessary and sufficient condition for almost sure convergence of a series of independent exponentially distributed random variables.

Ex 37 only emphasizes that the argument should use the Kolmogorov three-series theorem. Since Ex 13 was already solved by this route, Ex 37 is treated as a duplicate and is not solved again.
